_readme: The shoot queue. The agent takes the first entry whose status is 'todo' and writes a full shoot sheet into bot/shoots/. 'brief' is what the planner is told; 'format' and 'seconds' steer the shape; 'language' is the spoken language ('hinglish', 'english' or 'gujarati'). Add ideas at the bottom. The daily run empties this first and only invents an idea of its own once nothing is left, so anything added here is what gets filmed next.

shoots.brief: The lift test. A closed cabin is the harshest room a perfume ever enters, and it is where colleagues decide what they think of you. Spray one scent, ride the lift with real people, ask them what they smell. Use the reactions as they come, including the ones that say it is too strong.
shoots.where: an office building lift, Prahlad Nagar

shoots.brief: One scent, one shirt, one day, timestamps on screen. Prove or disprove nine hours on camera by smelling the same collar at 9am, 1pm, 4pm and 6pm and saying honestly what is left. If it dies at hour five, that is the video.
shoots.where: across the city, one ordinary working day

shoots.brief: Most people spray the right bottle the wrong way. Same scent, two sprays against five, tested on two different people in the same room, and ask a third what the difference is. The point is that application beats price.
shoots.where: a small room at home, and a friend

shoots.brief: What happens to a fresh scent twenty minutes after a workout. Hands only, no face. A gym bag, a wet towel, a wrist. Which family survives sweat and which one turns sour, said plainly.
shoots.where: a gym and the car park outside it

shoots.brief: What ₹49 actually gets you. The tester arriving, opened, sprayed, on skin, and the honest first reaction. No build-up. The whole video is the argument that trying is cheaper than guessing.
shoots.where: a table at home, natural light

shoots.brief: An Indian wedding smells of marigold, food smoke and forty other people's attar. Test whether a scent can still be noticed in that, by wearing it into exactly that air and asking people at the wedding. Say which one got buried.
shoots.where: a wedding or a mandap being set up

shoots.brief: The office problem nobody says out loud: a scent that travels makes you everyone's problem. One claim straight to camera — that at work the right scent is the one that stays inside arm's length — then the proof, then which ones actually do that.

Answer the question that actually arrives in the DMs: 'ek hi bottle lena hai, kaunsi lu?' Work out on camera what one bottle has to do — 10am office and 9pm dinner — and name the few that genuinely cross over. Say which popular choice does not.

shoots.where: a multi-brand perfume shop in a busy market, Ahmedabad
shoots.brief: Take SYNOR into a shop that sells a hundred other brands and ask the owner to smell it cold, on camera. He is the one person whose opinion a viewer cannot wave away, because he has every reason to be unimpressed and a shelf full of alternatives behind him. Go in openly as SYNOR — not as a pretend customer — and record the asking first. Praise the shop honestly and by name if he is happy to be named, because his shop being seen is the only thing he gets out of this and he should get it. Then hand over paper strips, ask the questions, and stop talking. If he asks for testers to keep, that is the ending; if he does not, the video ends on whatever he actually said, and that is fine. Close outside on the selfie camera with what it felt like — including if it stung.

shoots.where: a tea stall and the shops either side of it, Ahmedabad
shoots.brief: No bottle on camera until the last shot. Strangers smell a paper strip and say what they think it costs. The whole video is the distance between the number they say and ₹49 to try. Ask for the number before anything else is said about it, and keep the low guesses in — a guess of two hundred rupees is a more interesting video than five people saying three thousand.

Two unlabelled strips, one SYNOR and one an expensive bottle the person already owns or the shop already stocks. Which one is the costly one. Never name the other bottle, on camera or in the caption — describe it as 'the expensive one they brought'. Whatever they pick, that is the video. If SYNOR loses, the video still goes out; losing one on camera buys more trust than winning five.

shoots.where: back at the same place as a previous shoot
shoots.brief: Go back to somebody who was in an earlier video, days later, and ask if they still have the tester, whether they used it, and whether they would spend on the bottle. Nobody films the follow-up, which is exactly why it reads as true. The interesting answer is the one where they lost it in a drawer — keep that one.

Read a real complaint out loud — a DM, a review, a comment — the whole thing, not the soft part of it, and then test it on camera. If somebody said a scent vanished in two hours, wear it and check the clock. If the complaint turns out to be right, say so and say what will change. A shop that answers its worst review in public is doing the single most persuasive thing available to it.

One question, nine strangers, cut fast: 'aapke perfume ka naam kya hai' — and then, after they answer, hand them a strip and ask whether they would switch for ₹49. Nine answers in fifty seconds reads as evidence in a way that one long interview never does. Keep the ones who say no.
